analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks that keep mortgages on their own books from some consumer-lending rules.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by one senator with no cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a consumer-lending law passed after the 2008 financial crisis, the Truth in Lending Act. Banks that make a mortgage and hold it on their own books for the life of the loan would be immune from lawsuits for violating rules requiring lenders to check whether a borrower can afford the loan. Regulators would have to treat such loans as 'qualified mortgages,' and balloon-payment loans would qualify for that treatment even if they did not meet the usual requirements. Mortgage brokers who steer a borrower to such a loan would also be shielded from 'steering' lawsuits if they disclose that the bank plans to keep the loan.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions that originate mortgages and keep them on their balance sheets. They gain legal immunity from ability-to-repay lawsuits, looser standards that let them count balloon-payment loans as 'qualified mortgages,' and reduced regulatory scrutiny. Mortgage originators and brokers gain a shield from steering-liability suits on those loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks holding mortgages on their own books

how_it_helps.text: A depository institution that has held a residential mortgage on its balance sheet since origination cannot be sued for failing to comply with the Truth in Lending Act's ability-to-repay requirements, and banking regulators must treat the loan as a qualified mortgage.
The exemption survives if the bank later transfers the loan to another depository institution because of the originating bank's bankruptcy, failure, or purchase.
A mortgage originator is shielded from suit for steering a consumer if the depository institution plans to hold the loan for its life and the originator tells the consumer so.
Balloon-payment loans may qualify for the safe harbor even if they do not meet the usual qualified-mortgage requirements, under an explicit rule of construction in the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage borrowers, who could be placed in loans they cannot afford — including balloon-payment loans — with reduced ability to sue the lender or the broker afterward. Lenders keep the profits on bad loans while borrowers and, in a failure, regulators bear the downside.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage borrowers with less legal recourse

drawbacks.text: Borrowers would lose the right to sue a bank that put them in a loan they could not afford, so long as the bank kept the loan on its own books.

The bill explicitly lets balloon-payment loans qualify as 'qualified mortgages' even when they miss the standard requirements, making it easier to place borrowers in loans with a large final payment they may not be able to refinance or pay.

Supporters argue banks that keep loans on their books bear the default risk themselves, so they have an incentive to lend carefully, and that litigation costs over ability-to-repay rules can discourage portfolio lending; the bill removes that litigation exposure entirely rather than tailoring it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to lenders: immunity from lawsuits and looser qualified-mortgage treatment, including for balloon loans. The cost falls on borrowers, who would have less recourse if they were steered into an unaffordable loan. The bill's premise — that a bank holding its own loans lends prudently — is a real argument, but the bill does not condition the exemption on any standard of care; it simply removes liability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator David Perdue introduced the bill in the Senate on October 26, 2017.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage borrowers kept the existing ability-to-repay protections and the right to sue lenders who violate them; banks did not obtain the litigation exemption the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage borrowers, who kept their legal protections

for.name: Sen. David Perdue
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on October 26, 2017.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no other senator signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors.

industries.industry: Depository institutions (banks and credit unions making mortgage loans)
industries.note: The bill grants banks that hold mortgages on their own balance sheets immunity from ability-to-repay lawsuits and forces regulators to treat those loans as qualified mortgages, including balloon-payment loans that miss the usual requirements. The banks' gain — freedom from liability — is the borrower's loss of recourse.

Brokers who steer a consumer into a portfolio-held loan would be shielded from steering-liability suits by disclosing that the bank intends to keep the loan. Their gain is reduced liability to the very borrowers they advise.
